2 men arrested over suspected burglary at Prince William and Kate’s country home in eastern England

By: Danica Kirka, The Associated Press Posted: 7:31 AM EST Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026 Last Modified: 8:52 AM EST Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026

Advertisement

Advertise with us

  • Share
  • Print
  • Email
  • Read Later
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:27
Instaread

LONDON (AP) — Two men were arrested on the British royal family’s Sandringham estate, police said Tuesday, after a reported break-in at the country home of Prince William and Princess Catherine.

Norfolk Police said that officers were called Monday evening to reported “suspicious activity” at an address on the rural estate in eastern England. After a search involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter, two men were arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespassing.

The suspects were being held in custody Tuesday and hadn’t been charged.

Police said that “the property was unoccupied at the time of the incident.”

The Sun newspaper reported that masked men made their way into Anmer Hall on Monday night, when William, Kate and the rest of their family weren’t present.

William was in London on Tuesday and met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham for talks at 10 Downing St.

William and Kate’s Kensington Palace office said that it wouldn’t comment on security matters.

Anmer Hall, which has 10 bedrooms, was a wedding present to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II. William and Kate use the secluded red brick Georgian mansion about 110 miles (171 kilometers) north of London as a country residence on weekends. The couple and their three children spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, west of London, which they have described as their “forever home.”

Intruders have breached royal properties several times over the years.

In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate west of London and stole a pickup truck and a quad bike from a farm building. Charles and Queen Camilla weren’t at Windsor Castle at the time, but it was reported that William and Kate were in their nearby house.

Three years earlier, a man armed with a crossbow was detained on the castle grounds. Jaswant Singh Chail was later sentenced to nine years in prison after admitting he had been encouraged by a chatbot to kill Elizabeth.

In 1982, intruder Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the queen’s private chambers while she was in bed. The queen spent 10 minutes chatting with the burglar before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette.

Fagan was sent to a psychiatric hospital, then released and was later jailed for unrelated criminal offenses.

___

Jill Lawless contributed to this report.

A huge new London Museum tells the city’s story from the Romans to Banksy

Jill Lawless, The Associated Press 4 minute read 12:25 PM EST

LONDON (AP) — A Roman mosaic, a bloodstained shirt, a bagel filled with barbecued pork, a sewer-clogging chunk of fat.

These are just a few of the objects that help encapsulate Britain’s teeming capital at the London Museum, which bills itself as the world’s largest city museum.

The museum opens Saturday after a yearslong, 437-million-pound ($573-million) refurbishment of Victorian buildings that were once part of the city’s Smithfield meat market. It replaces the notoriously hard-to-find Museum of London, which was located half a mile (800 meters) away and closed in 2022.

The London Museum sits in a much more prominent location, between London’s financial district and the creative Clerkenwell area and next to the wholesale meat market, which is due to move elsewhere by 2030 after more than 800 years on the site.

Bob Woodward wants readers to know how he sees the world and how that shapes his reporting

Hillel Italie, The Associated Press 7 minute read Preview

Bob Woodward wants readers to know how he sees the world and how that shapes his reporting

Hillel Italie, The Associated Press 7 minute read Updated: 10:16 AM EST

WASHINGTON (AP) — After more than half a century as one of the world's most famous journalists, Bob Woodward still isn't quite used to being on the receiving end of an interview.

“If you ask something, I may naturally ask you a question,” says the 83-year-old author and longtime Washington Post reporter, adding that being a celebrity is "the reality, it is the TV media era, and you just deal with it.”

The average journalist doesn't live like Woodward, who spoke recently from the living room of the longtime residence he shares with his wife and fellow reporter, Elsa Walsh: a 19th-century Georgetown townhouse with enough grandeur to merit a profile in Architectural Digest. But he still identifies as a working journalist, ever curious about the story behind the headlines.

Woodward made his name in the 1970s as one of the defining outsiders, a recent hire at the Post who helped break the Watergate scandal and bring down President Richard Nixon. In the decades following, Woodward became a veritable brand for inside stories on Washington power, with a long run of bestselling books on the White House, the Supreme Court, the intelligence community and the military leadership. Denied access to Nixon, he has since met with sitting presidents from both major political parties, from Democrat Jimmy Carter to Republican Donald Trump, and has become as much a Washington fixture as the leaders of a given administration.

Music Review: Peter Gabriel contends with AI’s impact on being human in ‘o/i’

Krysta Fauria, The Associated Press 3 minute read Preview

Music Review: Peter Gabriel contends with AI’s impact on being human in ‘o/i’

Krysta Fauria, The Associated Press 3 minute read 6:04 AM EST

Like so many of us these days, Peter Gabriel is thinking a lot about artificial intelligence.

Specifically, as a handful of companies barrel toward creating hypothetical machine intelligence they hope surpasses our own, the 76-year-old singer and multi-instrumentalist is reflecting on what it means to be human.

On his latest album, “o/i,” the Genesis singer's response appears to be: Go outside, touch grass and remember that we are all “made of earth,” as he sings on one of the more upbeat tracks, “Who Are We Talking To?”

Much of the record, though, has a hypnotic solemnity that augments his message. “By the Nazarene with his Turing machine / I have been undone / By the mitochondria in my cells, by the ringing of the funeral bell / I have been undone,” he sings over staid synths reminiscent of a church organ on “Been Undone.”

New film adaptation of the sacred Hindu epic Ramayana sparks debate over authenticity

Deepa Bharath And Sheikh Saaliq, The Associated Press 7 minute read Preview

New film adaptation of the sacred Hindu epic Ramayana sparks debate over authenticity

Deepa Bharath And Sheikh Saaliq, The Associated Press 7 minute read Yesterday at 11:01 PM EST

LOS ANGELES (AP) — For many, the Ramayana is not just an epic with gods and superhumans shooting arrows, battling demons and zipping around in flying chariots.

Rather, it’s one of Hinduism’s foundational texts, whose stories, songs and prayers are a part of birth hymns, funeral rites and everything in between. The Ramayana’s retellings over millennia have transcended genre as well as national, religious, linguistic and cultural boundaries. It has also inspired religious and political movements — including the campaign for a grand temple honoring the epic's protagonist, Rama, in Ayodhya — that helped propel Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party into power.

Now, the epic tale — telling the story of Lord Rama defeating the demon king Ravana to rescue his wife Sita — is the subject of “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” released earlier this month to coincide with Diwali. Directed by filmmaker Nitesh Tiwari and the most expensive Indian film to ever be made, it synthesizes the star power of Bollywood, two Oscar-winning music composers and Hollywood visual effects in an ambitious attempt to bring one of India’s most revered stories to a global audience.

The film — whose second part is scheduled to be released next year — has sparked a global debate about its authenticity and faithfulness to traditional versions of the story.

“Focker In-Law” turns out to be a perfectly adequate sequel in large part thanks to adding something absolutely “Wicked” — Ariana Grande, who helps breathe new life into the moribund Focker Cinematic Universe.

Grande plays Olivia, a corporate coach and former FBI hostage negotiator who is the girlfriend to Greg Focker's son. She's flying in to New York for Robert De Niro’s birthday celebrations and to introduce herself to the dysfunctional clan.

This time, De Niro’s stern patriarch has softened into a vegan health nut who likes tofu and Pelotons. He cedes the antagonist role to Grande, who becomes the yin to Ben Stiller’s yang — a protective father who isn’t quite sold on his son’s angelic girlfriend.

“Grand Theft Auto VI” has gotten all kinds of attention since its release last week. It generated a record $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales. Pitchfork transformed music media. Founder Ryan Schreiber tells the story in ‘Weird Era’

Maria Sherman, The Associated Press 7 minute read Preview

Pitchfork transformed music media. Founder Ryan Schreiber tells the story in ‘Weird Era’

Maria Sherman, The Associated Press 7 minute read Updated: Yesterday at 9:16 AM EST

NEW YORK (AP) — You could call it catching lightning in a bottle or being in the right place at the right time. Or you could call it what it really was: powering up the family computer and unexpectedly transforming music media.

The year was 1996. In Minneapolis, a teenage music obsessive named Ryan Schreiber had an idea. Why not launch an online music zine published for and by enthusiasts with a strong point of view? Why not eventually call it something sharp, like Pitchfork?

He had no need for the neutrality of other early 'net adopters, like AllMusic, or legacy media like Rolling Stone's nascent online offerings. He wanted to differentiate his site through snark and smarts — and he had the youthful boldness to make it happen.

Or, to borrow a phrase from his memoir out Dec. 1, he understood that, “If you don't do it, someone else will. So why shouldn't it be you?”
